todays_goal: Solve percent problems accurately, explain evidence clearly, and use precise academic vocabulary.

lessons.subject: mathematics
lessons.lesson_title: Percent problem solving: part, percent, and whole
lessons.previous_learning: Friday was a half day. Percent-of-a-quantity work was mostly strong, but answers were inconsistent when the percent or the whole was unknown. Extra practice was used instead of advancing.
lessons.course_context: Consolidate the three core percent problem types before moving to more complex percent applications.
learning_objectives: Identify the part, percent, and whole in a percent problem.
Find a part when percent and whole are known.
Find a percent when part and whole are known.
Find a whole when part and percent are known.
Check whether a percent answer is reasonable.
lessons.why_it_matters: The same part-percent-whole structure appears in discounts, scores, data, tax, tips, and later proportional reasoning.

vocabulary.definition: the amount being compared with the whole
the complete amount
a rate per 100
the value being solved for
an equation showing two equivalent ratios
an answer whose size makes sense

lessons.written_instruction: For every problem, first label PART, PERCENT, and WHOLE and identify the unknown. To find a part, multiply the whole by the decimal form of the percent. To find the percent, divide part by whole and convert to a percent. To find the whole, divide the part by the decimal form of the percent.

independent_practice.prompt: Find 35% of 160.
Find 18% of 250.
Find 72% of 125.
28 is what percent of 80?
45 is what percent of 120?
54 is what percent of 90?
36 is 30% of what whole?
42 is 35% of what whole?
27 is 15% of what whole?
A $90 backpack is discounted by 20%. Find the discount and sale price.
A quiz has 48 correct answers out of 60 questions. What percent are correct?
A team has completed 65% of a 200-mile challenge. How many miles are complete?

exit_ticket.prompt: A $120 item is discounted by 15%. Find the discount and final price.
Explain how you decide whether to multiply or divide in a percent problem.
exit_ticket.answer: Identify the unknown: multiply percent by whole to find part; divide part by whole to find percent; divide part by decimal percent to find whole.

lessons.voice_prompt: Keep responses short. Before every percent problem, ask Atticus to label PART, PERCENT, WHOLE and identify the unknown. Model one example of each problem type, then let him work. For any assigned question, never give the final answer. If his attempt is wrong, identify only the setup step that needs repair, give one concise hint, and ask him to retry.
lessons.teacher_notes: Do not advance beyond core percent applications until unknown-percent and unknown-whole items are consistently correct.

lessons.subject: french
lessons.previous_learning: Thursday still showed confusion between descriptions and possession and inconsistent use of de after negative possession.
lessons.course_context: Keep the repair narrow and oral-first before adding more forms.
learning_objectives: Choose être for descriptions and avoir for possession.
Conjugate high-frequency forms accurately.
Form negative possession with ne/n'...pas de.
Answer orally in complete French sentences.
lessons.why_it_matters: Meaning-based verb choice and accurate negation are foundational for natural spoken and written French.

vocabulary.definition: what someone or something is like
having or owning something
to be
to have
ne...pas or n'...pas
many un, une, or des possession phrases become de after ne...pas

lessons.written_instruction: Decide whether each sentence expresses description/state or possession before choosing the verb. Use être for description and avoir for possession. In most negative possession statements, change un/une/des to de after ne...pas.

worked_examples.title: Description
worked_examples.explanation: Content is a description, so use être.

worked_examples.title: Possession
worked_examples.explanation: Having books is possession, so use avoir.

worked_examples.title: Negative possession
worked_examples.explanation: Use n'...pas around ai and change un to de.

guided_practice.prompt: Choose être or avoir: Ils ______ contents.
Choose être or avoir: Elles ______ trois livres.
Choose être or avoir: Nous ______ fatigués.

independent_practice.prompt: Make negative: J'ai un crayon.
Make negative: Elle a des devoirs.
Make negative: Nous avons une calculatrice.
Answer in French: Est-ce que tu as des devoirs aujourd'hui?
Answer in French: Est-ce que tu es fatigué aujourd'hui?

lessons.voice_prompt: Use oral-first practice and keep corrections concise. Before each item ask only: Description or possession? For assigned questions, never state the completed sentence. Give a meaning cue or point to the verb family and let Atticus produce the form.
lessons.teacher_notes: Require a correct description/possession decision before conjugation.

lessons.subject: literature
lessons.previous_learning: Thursday showed good plot understanding and improving motivation analysis, but theme evidence still needs significance rather than simple event listing.
lessons.course_context: Continue full Grade 6 fiction while requiring evidence that actually proves an inference or theme.
learning_objectives: Infer a character's motivation from actions and dialogue.
Write a universal theme statement.
Choose evidence that supports a theme.
Explain the significance of evidence.
Write an objective summary.
lessons.why_it_matters: Evidence-based inference and theme analysis support later literary essays and discussion.

vocabulary.definition: why a character chooses an action
a conclusion based on evidence plus reasoning
a universal message developed by a story
a specific detail supporting an interpretation
what the evidence proves or reveals
a short factual account of the main events

lessons.written_instruction:
Read The Second Envelope twice. After citing any evidence, complete the idea: This matters because it shows... Motivation must name what a character wants, fears, avoids, protects, or hopes to gain. Theme must be universal rather than character-specific.

On Tuesday morning, Elena found two envelopes taped beneath the debate club's supply box. One was labeled FINAL TOPICS. The other was labeled BACKUP TOPICS - OPEN ONLY IF NEEDED. The club's practice tournament began after lunch. During third period, Marcus suggested opening the backup list early so they could practice both possible topics. Elena refused because opening it would make it no longer a true backup. At lunch, the teacher announced that a printer error had revealed one final topic and the backup list would now be used. Marcus said, Good thing we didn't open it. Elena later explained that sometimes keeping an option useful means not using it early. Every team then received the same new topic at the same time.

worked_examples.title: Motivation
worked_examples.problem: A student hides a broken device before inspection.
worked_examples.solution: The student may want to avoid blame or embarrassment.
worked_examples.explanation: Motivation explains why the action is chosen.

worked_examples.title: Significance
worked_examples.problem: Evidence: the student later reports the problem before anyone is hurt.
worked_examples.solution: This shows responsibility can require admitting a mistake.
worked_examples.explanation: The significance connects the event to the interpretation.

independent_practice.prompt: What temptation does Marcus present to Elena?
What is Elena trying to protect when she refuses to open the backup envelope?
Why does the printer error make Elena's earlier decision important?
What can you infer about Elena from her actions? Use one exact detail.
Write one universal theme statement.
Give TWO pieces of evidence for your theme. After each, explain its significance.
Write a 3-sentence objective summary.

exit_ticket.prompt: Choose one event from the story. Explain why it is strong or weak evidence for your theme.
exit_ticket.answer: Answers vary; evidence is strong when it directly supports the theme and its significance is explained.

lessons.voice_prompt: Keep the reading at Grade 6. After Atticus cites a detail, ask one short question: What does that prove? Do not reveal a theme or provide wording for assigned answers. If his evidence is weak, explain what type of evidence would be stronger without giving the exact event.
lessons.teacher_notes: Score literal comprehension separately from evidence/significance quality.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.lesson_title: Filters, available light, and object color
lessons.previous_learning: Friday's filter predictions were generally good, but the exit response did not accurately state the filter's role as a selective transmitter.
lessons.course_context: Complete the color/filter model by tracking light from source to filter to object to eye.
learning_objectives: Explain a colored filter as a selective transmitter.
Identify available light after a filter.
Predict object appearance under filtered light.
Distinguish selective transmission from selective reflection.
lessons.why_it_matters: A correct source-filter-object-eye model explains why the same object can appear different under different lighting.

vocabulary.definition: a material that transmits some wavelengths more strongly than others
letting some wavelengths pass more strongly than others
the wavelengths or colors present after the source and filter
an object reflecting some wavelengths more strongly
take in light energy
a representation used to explain or predict

lessons.written_instruction: Use the sequence source -> filter -> object -> eye. A filter selectively transmits some wavelengths and absorbs much of the rest; it does not create color. First identify the light available after the filter, then predict what the object can reflect.

worked_examples.title: Blue filter and white card
worked_examples.problem: White light passes through a blue filter and reaches white paper.
worked_examples.explanation: The filter transmits more blue light; white paper reflects the available blue light.

independent_practice.prompt: What does a red filter do to white light? Use transmit and absorb.
White light passes through a green filter and shines on white paper. Predict the paper's appearance and explain.
White light passes through a blue filter and shines on a red object. Why might the object look dark?
Explain the difference between selective transmission by a filter and selective reflection by an object.
Draw and label a source -> filter -> object -> eye model for a red filter shining on a white card.

exit_ticket.prompt: A colored filter changes which wavelengths are ______ for the object to reflect.
Explain why a filter does not make an object a new color.
exit_ticket.answer: The filter changes which wavelengths are available; appearance still depends on which available wavelengths the object reflects and absorbs.

lessons.voice_prompt: Teach source -> filter -> object -> eye. Require Atticus to name the available light after the filter before predicting appearance. For assigned questions, never state the final prediction; ask which wavelengths are available and what the object tends to reflect.
lessons.teacher_notes: If exit is secure, Light and Materials can move toward unit synthesis/assessment.

lessons.subject: history_geography
lessons.lesson_title: Persian Wars: cooperation among rival poleis
lessons.previous_learning: Thursday showed a strong direct-versus-representative democracy comparison and accurate context about exclusion in Athens.
lessons.course_context: Move from internal Greek political systems to a shared external threat that sometimes encouraged cooperation among independent poleis.
learning_objectives: Explain why independent poleis might form an alliance.
Connect geography to military strategy.
Distinguish alliance from political unification.
Explain how a common threat can temporarily change relations among rivals.
lessons.why_it_matters: The Persian Wars show that politically independent communities can cooperate without becoming one government.

vocabulary.definition: a large ancient empire east of the Greek world
organized entry of armed forces into another territory
an agreement to cooperate for a shared purpose
a plan for achieving a goal
a narrow passage of water connecting larger bodies of water
work together toward a shared goal

lessons.written_instruction: Read for cause and effect rather than memorizing dates. By the early 400s BCE, the Persian Empire controlled a large area east of the Greek world. Greek poleis were politically independent and often rivals, but a shared external threat could encourage alliances. Mountains constrained land movement while the Aegean Sea and narrow waterways could shape strategy. Cooperation did not erase separate governments or old rivalries.

worked_examples.title: Alliance vs unification
worked_examples.solution: They are cooperating, not necessarily politically unified.
worked_examples.explanation: An alliance can be temporary while each polis keeps its own government.

independent_practice.prompt: Why did the size of the Persian Empire create a challenge for individual Greek poleis?
How could Greek geography affect military strategy?
Why might rival poleis form an alliance even if they did not trust one another completely?
Does forming an alliance mean the poleis became one unified government? Explain.
What larger idea does the Persian Wars example add to what you learned about cultural connection and political independence?

exit_ticket.prompt: In 3-4 sentences, explain why politically independent communities might cooperate temporarily during a shared crisis.
exit_ticket.answer: They may share a threat or goal larger than their rivalry, coordinate resources or strategy, and still keep separate governments.

lessons.voice_prompt: Focus on cause/effect and geography, not battle-date memorization. Keep explanations concise. For assigned questions, ask Atticus to name the threat, reason for cooperation, or geographic factor rather than giving the full response.
lessons.teacher_notes: Do not equate alliance with political unification.

lessons.subject: writing
lessons.previous_learning: Thursday's analytical writing had a valid idea but repeated the same compromise point several times. Exact evidence and sentence boundaries are improving.
lessons.course_context: Increase analytical precision by requiring two genuinely different evidence points and reasoning after each.
learning_objectives: Write a clear claim.
Use two different exact details as evidence.
Explain the significance of each detail.
Avoid repetitive reasoning.
Use complete sentence boundaries.
lessons.why_it_matters: Analytical writing is stronger when each sentence adds new evidence or reasoning rather than restating the same point.

vocabulary.definition: the point being proved
a specific detail supporting the claim
why the evidence supports the claim
why a detail matters
specific and exact
unnecessary reuse of the same idea or wording

lessons.written_instruction: Use claim -> evidence -> reasoning. Then add a second, different evidence point and new reasoning. Each sentence should add something new. Revise run-ons before submitting.

worked_examples.title: Repetitive
worked_examples.problem: The choice was responsible. It was a responsible choice because it was responsible.
worked_examples.explanation: The sentences repeat the same idea without adding evidence or reasoning.

worked_examples.title: Improved
worked_examples.problem: Elena kept the backup envelope sealed. When the original topic was compromised, the unused backup could be given to every team fairly.
worked_examples.explanation: The second sentence adds a consequence that explains why the evidence matters.

independent_practice.prompt: Write one precise evidence sentence from The Second Envelope.
Write one reasoning sentence explaining what that evidence proves.
Write a second DIFFERENT piece of evidence and reasoning.
Repair this run-on: Elena wanted to win she also wanted the tournament to be fair she kept the envelope sealed.

Write 8-10 sentences answering: Why was keeping the backup envelope sealed a responsible decision? Include a claim, TWO different exact details, reasoning after each detail, and a conclusion. Avoid repeating the same idea in different words.

lessons.voice_prompt: Keep help concise. Do not supply sentences for Atticus to copy. If evidence is vague, ask: What exact event or line are you using? If reasoning repeats the claim, ask: What does this detail prove that the claim alone does not? For assigned writing, never dictate the final wording.

lessons.subject: computer_science
lessons.previous_learning: Thursday showed major improvement in generalization and overfitting. The remaining concept is why separate test data provides a fair measure of new-example performance.
lessons.course_context: Move from qualitative model evaluation to simple percentage accuracy on held-out test data.
learning_objectives: Calculate test accuracy as correct predictions divided by total predictions.
Compare training and test accuracy.
Explain why test data must remain separate from training data.
Connect a training-test gap to generalization and overfitting.
Explain why sample size matters.
lessons.why_it_matters: A model should be judged on new examples, not only the examples it already learned from.

vocabulary.definition: the fraction or percent of predictions that are correct
separate examples used to evaluate a trained model
performing well on new examples
performing well on training examples but poorly on new examples
testing on data not used to teach the model
the number of examples included in a test

lessons.written_instruction: Accuracy = correct predictions / total predictions x 100%. Use a held-out test set to estimate performance on unseen examples. A large training-test gap may suggest weak generalization or overfitting.

worked_examples.title: Test accuracy
worked_examples.problem: 18 of 20 new test images are correct.

worked_examples.title: Training-test gap
worked_examples.explanation: The model performs much worse on new examples than on training examples.

independent_practice.prompt: A model gets 17 of 20 separate test images correct. Write the accuracy calculation and percent.
A model gets 45 of 50 test examples correct. Find test accuracy.
Model A: training 99%, test 97%. Model B: training 100%, test 58%. Which model shows stronger generalization? Explain.
Why is test accuracy more useful than training accuracy for judging performance on new examples?
Why can a very small test set give a misleading picture of model quality?

exit_ticket.prompt: Write the formula for accuracy in words.
exit_ticket.answer: Correct predictions divided by total predictions, multiplied by 100%.

exit_ticket.prompt: Explain why the test set must remain separate from training data.
exit_ticket.answer: The model must be evaluated on examples it did not learn from so the test measures generalization rather than memory of training examples.

lessons.voice_prompt: Keep the explanation short and concrete. Connect accuracy to percent math. For assigned calculations, confirm only the setup, not the final percentage. For conceptual questions, use one analogy at most and then ask Atticus to restate the idea.
lessons.teacher_notes: If exit is secure, advance next to error analysis rather than repeating overfitting.

answer_key.cs-i4: Test accuracy measures performance on unseen data; training accuracy can reflect memorization.
answer_key.cs-i5: A few examples can be unrepresentative, so one or two results can swing the percentage strongly.
